Label: Road to Bhabua
Description: The road from Chand village continues on to the town of Bhabhua, which Bhabhua (or Kaimur) district headquarters. The road is an important area traffic artery.  The crossroads with the main road from Chainpur serves as an essential bus stand.

Label: Get your bike repaired
Description: Bicycle repairman Malik Sharma stood in his shop with one of his sons.  Business has been good near the bus stand given that scores of bicycles join the other traffic traversing the main road and the roads leading to it from north and south.  At this time, Malik was head of Chainpur’s local shaka (branch) of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (National Volunteer Society or RSS) promoting Hindu nationalist sentiments.

Label: See Malik do puja
Description: Malik Sharma offered incense to the deities Lakshmi, Ganesh, and Saraswati through the picture he has placed in a box in his shop that he has labelled “temple of Mother.”  Another image of the trio can be seen below while at right he has hung an image of Vishvakarma, patron god of artisans and craftworkers.  Malik has named his shop after the deity as seen on the sign atop the roof.

Label: Find medication for leprosy and tuberculosis
Description: The wall-painted sign advertised for the local public hospital: “Everyone can get for free T.B. and leprosy medication at the government hospital.  Varanasi Service Center, Adhaura” [the latter refers to the bloc where the hospital stood].

Label: Thana to Chand village road
Description: The road from the town of Bhabhua to the village of Chand has been an important area traffic artery.  The crossroads with the main road from Chainpur has served as an essential bus stand.  However, at the turn of the century, the road was narrow at best and often suffered from vast potholes and crumbling pavement.  Shepherds lead their flock, sharing the well-worn road with towering Tata trucks.

Label: A to B
Description: The main road to Chainpur led from the bazaar around the bus stand through fields and into Chainpur’s main bazaar.

Label: See a roadside tool maker and seller
Description: This storeowner and craftsman offered a variety of tools for home and agricultural use.  He fashioned wood implements and wood handles for metal tools.

Label: Buy some tools
Description: Wooden rolling pins, hand blenders, and chapati rolling platforms can be purchased from this artisan along with metal ladles, bowls, and hoes.

Label: See Sri Gauri Shankar Mahadev Mandir (“temple”)
Description: A person wearing a cricket outfit has passed the entrance to a temple dedicated to the goddess Gauri and the gods Shiv and Vishnu.  The road pavement has disintegrated unevenly along its edges.  Devotees would make much effort to improve the temple in the coming decades.

Label: See the mandir and an open well
Description: The temple precinct’s open ground occasionally has served as a useful site to gather and work harvested crops.  However, workers carefully have kept respectfully clean the raised concrete plinth in the left background with its Shiv linga and accompanying image of Shiv’s devotee, Nandi the bull.  In the foreground was an open well of a sort necessary before tube wells gave easier access to aquifer water sources.

Label: See agricultural fields
Description: Villages are defined as much by the fields that surround them as by their habitations and other buildings.  Unsurprisingly, almost any land without a building on it is tilled, seeded, and harvested, as could be seen at right along the roadside.

Label: View a set of Sufi Muslim tombs
Description: Enclosed by the white-washed protective walls were the tombs of two Sufis (revered Islamic figures).

Label: See the established mazars (“tombs”) of two Sufis
Description: Two white-washed barrows have marked the burial place of the two Sufis while the wall helped both maintain the cleanliness of the site and make it more visible.

Label: See a visual expression of Islamic practice
Description: Beneath a depiction of the Kaba in Makkah and the dome of the Prophet’s Mosque in Madinah two of the most popular pilgrimage sites for Muslims worldwide were the Urdu words (from right to left) for fasting (roza), prayer (namaz), the profession of faith (tauhid), alms (zakat), and pilgrimage (hajj) to Makkah.  Notably, the words have emerged from the flames of dips, oil-fed lamps devotionally used by both Muslims and Hindus in South Asia.

Label: See the construction of Sufi mazars (“tombs”)
Description: This platform with its two barrows indicating the tombs of two Sufis has been under construction.  A Hindu devotee has cared for the tombs, maintaining their tidiness.  Practices involving Sufis, living and dead, have frequently involved a mélange of devotees drawn from different religious communities.

Label: See a mark of devotion
Description: Devotees sometimes have marked their devotion to a dead Sufi by adorning a mazar with a chadar (“sheet”) covered in Islamic texts and/or images.

Label: B to FF
Description: A cycle rickshaw driver laboriously pedalled his customers on the road leading from Chowk in Chainpur to the bus stand.  This was the northern edge of the habitations and businesses in the most densely settlement of the village.

Label: See Islamic decorations
Description: A clockface chalked on this store’s door helped advertise the Golden Watch business.  The Islamic symbol of a crescent moon with star hung above a similarly chalked image of the Taj Mahal in Agra.  The artist included a view of the garden in which this most iconic of Indian buildings stands.  Meanwhile, the Arabic numbers above the door (“786”) have long represented the Islamic system of abjad that assigns letters in words to numbers as a form of religious arithmetic.  “786” has been particularly auspicious.

Label: Consider family planning
Description: This ruined wall painting counseled Indians to decrease population growth and used the nation-wide family planning icon of a family of four woman, man, boy, girl as a model of the “small family is a happy family” motto.  In 1952, India was among the first nations to initiate a voluntary family planning program for its whole population, although forced and pressured sterilizations of millions have occurred in two different periods since then.

Label: FF to B
Description: The corner of a mud-plastered, stone-walled home has collapsed on the left, necessitating repairs.  Newer homes and businesses increasingly have relied on brick, as seen with the surrounding buildings.  Although the road has been paved, accumulated wear and earth causes muddy puddles to form after rainstorms.

Label: FF to EE
Description: As some residents stared at the foreign ethnographer photographing the scene, others passed the increasingly dense group of shops that constitute Chainpur’s main bazaar as they walk the main road toward the intersection known as Chowk.

Label: See a family store
Description: The Agrawal family has run this shop for decades.  Earlier, they only developed photographic film and made photocopies, representing the only local business to do so.  But in the 1990s, the Agrawals added the first international telephone booth in Chainpur.

Label: Read the store’s main sign
Description: “Agrawal Studios – artist and photographer” “Chainpur, Kaimur (Bhabhua) district” “Our store can make black & white and color photos beautiful and clean” “Our store is a photographic service for weddings and preparations” “Photo framing available here.”

Label: Enter Agrawal studio
Description: Sanjit Agrawal offers much more than film, photocopying, and telephone services.  He also makes identification photos, takes family photos, and sells devotional items.  The top shelf holds framed portraits of (from right to left) Mohandas (“Mahatma”) Gandhi, K.S. Hedgewar (founder of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh or RSS), and M.S. Golwalker (second leader of the RSS).

Label: Buy a devotional item
Description: Alongside shelves with images of the Islamic figure Buraq (lower left) and the Hindu Devi (center left), stood those (upper left) with images of Durga, Hanuman, Kali, and the local Harsu Brahm as well as murtis (statues) of Lakshmi and Ganesh used by these like other Hindu storeowners for daily puja.  Below this stood an image of B.R. Ambedkar, the freedom fighter who authored India’s Constitution and led the Dalit (“crushed”) movement.

Label: Use the store’s telecommunications
Description: “STD (Subscriber Trunk Dialing)” “ISD (International Direct Dialing)” “PCO (Public Call Office)” [These three services provided, respectively, national, international, and local telephone calling] “National and international specific telephone service and telephone [remainder obscured by poster]”

Label: See locally made fuel
Description: These dried patties were made from a mixture of straw and gobar (“cow dung”).  Although their smoke when burned in homes proved unhealthy, they have remained an inexpensive fuel source for those who cannot afford electricity or natural gas.  Each bore the hand print of its maker.

Label: See a sign for an Islamic school
Description: The sign advertised an Islamic elementary school (maktab) where children learn Quranic reading and recitation, among other schools.  It stands behind the buildings seen here.

Label: Get a kurta made
Description: Muhammad Adil has sat at his pedal-powered sewing machine, able to tailor even during the frequent failures of the electrical supply.  He wore a lungi (waist cloth) to keep cool in the heat.

Label: Read the tailor shop’s sign
Description: “Village Kurta Tailor Master” in Hindi.

Label: Visit a carpentry shop
Description: Bhagat Kumar stood in front of his carpentry shop awaiting customers.  Like many buildings in Chainpur, this had walls plastered by dried mud and a roof of baked clay tiles.

Label: Enter the carpentry shop
Description: Bhagat Kumar has sat among the various tools of his carpentry trade and some of his projects.

Label: EE to C
Description: A boy has taken a pushcart past a Jeep parked by an Islamic masjid (mosque) and a Hindu mandir (temple) that have long stood opposite one another.

Label: Visit the Shiv mandir (“temple”)
Description: This small Shiv mandir has stood nearly opposite a masjid and has demonstrated common features to the area’s other temples.

Label: View the front of the mandir
Description: Although small, this temple has followed a common north Indian pattern of a porch-like entrance (mandapa) preceding the main, mountain-shaped garbhagriha in which the central deity has resided.

Label: See the linga and yoni
Description: The linga and the yoni in which it has for centuries represented Shiv and Devi, and their union.  Nandi the bull has been Shiv’s loyal devotee while above a bell has hung for the use of devotees who announce their presence when entering.

Label: View other murtis (statues)
Description: On the wall beyond the the Shiv linga and the yoni has stood murtis (statues) of other deities such as Ganesh and Hanuman.  A small stand to the right held burnt incense sticks lit by devotee as an act of veneration.
Notes: photo matched approximately: C to EE mandir garbagriha details 2000s

Label: Visit the masjid
Description: One of Chainpur’s mosques can be found in the busy main bazaar.  The mosque was associated with the Deobandi movement while others were Barelvi.  Typical for much of north India, only men pray in Chainpur’s mosques while women, and many men, do so at home.

Label: Enter the prayer space
Description: As one entered into the masjid, one would pass a handpump installed to aid those washing before going to namaz (daily prayers).  To the right of the door, a paper listed the different prayer times, which change over the course of a week due to changes in sunrise and sunset.

Label: Look to the right
Description: The shelves to the let hold copies of the Quran for anyone’s use while the empty shelves on the right wait to receive the shoes of those entering the mosque to pray.  Hindus also remove their shoes when entering temples while devotees of all religious belongings go barefoot or in socks when approaching a Sufi tomb.

Label: View the length of the prayer area
Description: The antechamber that precedes the innermost interior of the masjid (mosque) serves also as a prayer space, as evident by the woven mats laid on the floor in preparation for devotees placing their prayer rugs on top.  Seats to perform ritual washing before prayers stood at left.

Label: See where wuzu was done
Description: Wuzu (Arabic: wudu) involved the ritual washing of feet, hands, and face before namaz (daily prayers).  Prayer goers have perched pitchers above the trough to use.

Label: View a minar (minaret)
Description: Minars (prayer towers) commonly have accompanied masjids in South Asia even when only decorative as here.  Originally intended centuries ago as heights from which the muezzin makes the call to prayer (azan), minars have become less important with the advent of loudspeakers (although sometimes these are placed in the minar).

Label: See the muezzin make the call to prayer
Description: A muezzin (one who makes the azan) in another Chainpur mosque would make the azan (call to prayer; Arabic: adhan) using an electrified loudspeaker perched atop the minar five times daily, as has been Sunni Islamic custom.

Label: Buy fruit from a pushcart
Description: Pushcarts have offered merchants the mobility to sell fruits, vegetables, or other goods along every street and gali (alley) in the village.

Label: A great deal of Chainpur’s socializing centers on chai (tea).  Hosts
Description: other than some who can’t afford it routinely serve chai to visitors to their homes.  In public spaces, chai dukhans (shops) prove central gathering places for communing, conversation, news, and gossip.  Balu keeps busy ensuring that the chai is piping hot and the snacks are freshly made.

Label: Meet the chai dukhan’s customers
Description: The presence of Imran Khan, Vijay Singh, M. Adil Khan, and Vikesh Singh among Balu’s customers reflects how Hindus and Muslims and even sometimes Sikhs commonly share one another’s company in such social spaces.

Label: Visit a medicine shop
Description: Suresh Choudhari completed his studies at Banaras Hindu University (BHU) and returned home to Chainpur to open this medical store.  Surrounded by shelves full of medicines, he has hung above where he sat a portrait of Chandrashekhar Azad, an Indian freedom fighter who died in 1931 while leading armed resistance against British rule in the previous years.

Label: Read the store’s sign
Description: “Choudhari Medical Hall” “Chainpur, Kaimur-Bhabhua” “Note English, Ayurvedic, and homeopathic veterinary medicines also can be found here.”

Description: In Chainpur, signs of agricultural activity are seldom far out of sight.  Goats feed while a motorcycle roars past.  An orange-painted mandir (“temple”) stands across the street from a white-washed masjid (“mosque”).

Label: C to V
Description: Heading east from this intersection leads one past a corner chai dukhan (“tea shop”) and down this paved road to the muhalla (“neighborhood”) of Sonahtiya.  A child clutches a kite prepared to fly.

Label: C to GG
Description: A man watches a photographer while standing on the brick-paved but potholed road to Chainpur’s Chowk Bazaar wearing a sports shirt and pants.  In the distance, another man wears a lungi wrapped around his hips and reaching his ankles as well as a scarf-like strip of cloth around his shoulders is a gamcha, the telltale piece of apparel that comes in various colors and indicates a Bihari man who works as a farmer.

Label: Visit a purohit (ritual specialist) serving the Harsu Brahm mandir (“temple”)
Description: Ramesh Tripathi sits outside his family’s home business with his brother Sitaram, awaiting those who need his services at the village’s most important mandir (“temple”) down the road.

Label: Read an advertisement for services offered by a family of pujaris (ritual specialists)
Description: Opposite advertisements for telecom services they offer (“STD” (Subscriber Trunk Dialing) “ISD” (International Direct Dialing) “PCO” (Public Call Office) the advertisement offers that “This is a beautiful and clean place for pilgrims to stay. Every facility is here.”

Label: See a Bollywood film poster
Description: Among the vast array of characters in the epic Ramayan found in Sanskrit, Hindi, and other languages, Ravan has stood out in many as the arch-rival of Ram, avatar of Vishnu.  This poster advertises a Hindi-language film that showed in a Bhabhua theater with a modern Ravan as its central figure.

Label: See biris being made
Description: Amir, a biri maker, works all day, perhaps earning 25 rupees if he can make as many as one thousand by rolling chopped tobacco into a leaf.

Label: See Amir work
Description: Amir must first chop the tobacco into small bits, then wrap them into a tobacco leaf, before tying it tightly so it will not unwind.  When lit, biris produce a pungent, unfiltered smoke favored particularly by those who can’t afford cigarettes.

Label: Meet a temple ritual specialist
Description: Siddharth Nath, a pujari (Hindu ritual specialist) writes his devotion across his house, with the names “Radhakrishna” and “Sitaram” painted repeatedly under the roof’s eaves and “Ram” painted in the small alcove in the wall.  He wears a gamcha a scarf particular to Bihari men slung over his shoulder.

Label: GG to C
Description: Wearing a green sari with an orange bodice, this woman is one of the relative few walking through the bazaar.  Chainpur’s public spaces tended to be used by men with women of higher status economic status often restricted to home as an expression of that status.  Women who worked outside could not be held within such limits.

Label: GG to AA
Description: The closer to Chowk Bazaar, the denser the businesses become.  Stores for cloth, readymade clothing, paan, and home goods are all on display for those passing by.

Label: Enter a barber shop
Description: Faisal Yacqub sits in front of his barber shop under the shade of a thatched roof.  His shop bears the marks of public health measures such as the record of an application of the pesticide DDT to the right of the door and the handwritten adage on the wall around the corner “India made this pledge: To eliminate leprosy.”  Leprosy victims in the Chainpur area don’t face the stigma found in other places in India, expediting their cure.

Label: Get a haircut

Label: Visit a woman-run business

Description: Sita Ma oversaw work while sitting at right while Shukla made sweets at left.  Her white sari may indicate that she has been widowed. Label: Visit a cloth store and social place
Description: The Chaurasiya family has run this cloth and readymade clothing store for two generations.  It has served not only as a thriving business but as a social place for sharing news, views, and chai, especially among the storeowner’s friends.  A tailor offered services for those buying cloth, working his pedal-powered sewing machine.

Label: See the store’s role as a social place
Description: Friends of the storeowner, Arvind Chaurasiya, routinely stopped by to relax on the mattress-covered floor, reading newspapers and discussing current events even as customers came in and out transacting business without religious or jati (caste) distinction.  Cloth merchants commonly travelled along the Ganga River Valley endeavoring to maintain their stock’s diversity.

Label: See respect for an elder
Description: Above the shelves packed with merchandise, Arvind had hung a framed photograph of his father who previously ran the store.  It has been garlanded with a mala (a string of flowers) in a common gesture of reverence.

Label: See the shop’s puja place
Description: Hindu merchants commonly place in their shops a pair of Lakshmi (left) and Ganesh (right) murtis (statues), dedicating a new set of murtis each Diwali holiday after cleaning out their shop thoroughly and often applying a fresh coat of whitewash inside and out.  Lakshmi is the Goddess of Wealth and Ganesh the Remover of Obstacles.  Behind the shrine appeared to be a picture of the deity couple Kirshna and Radha.

Label: See a Durga poster
Description: Hundreds of millions of Hindus worship Durga (seen at center) or one of the many other manifestations of this devi (goddess).  Many devotees understand her as a fearsome antagonist of chaos and, at the same time, a loving mother figure.  In one narrative, the gods arm her with their separate, distinctive weapons because none of them could overwhelm a buffalo demon causing havoc. She ultimately subdues him, but not before transforming into the even fiercer Kali.

Label: See a Hanuman poster
Description: In the renowned epic Ramayan, the great god-hero Ram and his brother Lakshman fall dead to the overwhelming onslaught of their enemy Ravan, a powerful rakshas (demon).  Hanuman, Ram's devoted monkey follower, hears that a cure can be found on a Himalayan peak.  Through his tremendous strength, Hanuman carries the entire mountain vegetation and all to revive the brothers.  Many Hindus revere Hanuman as a paragon of devotion and heroism.

Label: Buy incense

Label: Visit a shop selling pamphlets and pictures

Description: The Harsu Brahm Dham (abode) has capped the top of the qila (fort), demonstrating the victory of a Brahman’s vengeful ghost over Raja (ruler) Salivahan whom he once served as vizier (advisor).  Although the temple’s precincts have enclosed a large space within its white walls, its steeple did not appear very prominently.  In front of it has stood the ochre-painted Shiv temple and a metal-roofed havan (fire sacrifice place).

Label: Visit the Harsu Brahm Dham (Abode])
Description: Perhaps the young person here awaited family members who have respectfully removed their sandals before entering Harsu Brahm Dham.  The temple’s designers have established a Ganesh murti (material form) above the entranceway and the auspicious syllable Aum (or Om) above that.

Label: Enter the dham
Description: Devotees customarily ring a bell when entering temples to call the attention of the deity.  Beyond the archway to the right was the firepit used to burn the offerings made to Harsu Brahm.  Ahead was the interior of the dham that houses the murti (material expression) of Harsu Brahm.  The temple courtyard stood to the left.  Because turning one’s back to a murti would be disrespectful to the deity, devotees would exit the temple by moving backwards.

Label: See devotees doing puja
Description: Three large festivals occur at Harsu Brahm Dham every year during which pilgrims stream from buses and private vehicles as well as on foot into the crowded courtyard to spend time in his presence, sitting in the courtyard facing his murti (material form).  During the birthday celebration of Shastri Brahm, a descendent of Harsu Brahm's personal purohit arrives an officiates at a service important for many Chainpur area residents.

Label: See Harsu Brahm’s murti
Description: Harsu Brahm’s murti (material form) is a stone.  He took this form after his unjust death when he returned to Chainpur’s qila as a brahm (vengeful Brahman ghost).  This murti provides a focus for the devotee's attentions when in the temple.  The Brahman here acted as a purohit (sacrifier), the person qualified to perform the ritual, for a patron.  Because the patron actually would take responsibility for the financial and other costs of the ritual and would gain the merit from the action, they would be the sacrificer.

Label: See the dham’s courtyard
Description: Often a crowd would fill the courtyard of the dham, small groups of family members awaiting their turn to interact with the deity as mediated through a purohit (sacrifier).

Label: View memorials left by devotees
Description: The memorials have born witness to the satisfaction which a visit to Harsu Brahm Dham has prompted for many devotees and pilgrims.  These were of four types.  The first was an inscribed stone recording the devotee's name. The second was a pinda (mound) usually of stone.  Third was a murti (material expression) of Shiv, with whom the brahm sometimes has been associated, which takes the shape of an image, linga, or symbol.  Finally, and very uncommonly, someone may have a statue of them placed so as to suggest their constant devotional presence. The red box accepted donations for the maintenance of the dham.

Label: See the havan
Description: The havan has served as a specially designed pit where Brahmanic fire sacrifices have been made.  Vedic fire sacrifice dates to at least three thousand years ago. Fire, personified as the god Agni, has been considered by many Hindus since ancient times to be the carrier of devotions to the deities.

Label: See the southern edge of Chainpur
Description: Chainpur’s southern habitations effectively end at the fort with mostly its fields stretching beyond.  In the dim distance is the start of the Kaimur Hills, which are part of the northern edge of India’s central Deccan Plateau.

Label: View agricultural life
Description: The geography of Chainpur’s immediate environ have long been dominated by inhabitated places, agricultural lands, and the hills of the Kaimur Plateau.  Farmers have separated fields with earthen embankments that also have served as trails between the crops.  Rain runoff from the Kaimur Hills have watered the fields, thus helping the area’s agricultural success.

Label: View a village and it fields
Description: The trees of this small village between Chainpur and the towering cliffs of the Kaimur Hills have offered shade and products (like coconuts and sap for toddy) to the residents when they have taken a break from working their fields.  The crop would be harvested after some months.

Label: See a sap tapper
Description: Some village residents would climb a palm tree to tap its sap in order to make toddy, a folk alcoholic drink that became illegal.

Label: See an ox-team plow
Description: Although cultivators increasingly have relied on tractors, ox teams (along with water buffalo teams) still have served as central for much farming, churning the soil in preparation for seeding. LINK TO TRACTOR

Label: Watch the paddy being moved
Description: The cultivation of wet rice a major crop for Chainpur (as for India in general) requires the laborious replanting of the paddy (young rice stalks).

Label: View the harvest
Description: Men and women labored here to cut and bring in the masur (lentil) harvest.  Labor-intensive agricultural work has employed the majority of Chainpur area residents for generations.

Label: See water buffalo
Description: Water buffalo have provided crucial resources of milk and labor.  These have returned from time wallowing in a pond or tank.

Label: In keeping with the RSS’s Hindu nationalism, each school day began with children reciting prayers facing this altar with its garlanded images of the auspicious syllable Aum (or Om) and of Ma Bharat (Mother India), which conflated the devi’s person with the territory of India. Description: Children frequently run to the bazaar on an errand for a parent or other family member.

Label: See Chainpur’s congregational mosque
Description: Although a Sunni Muslim community may use many mosques in its vicinity, most male members would gather for the special Friday noon prayer at the Jama Masjid (congregational mosque).

Label: See Muslims perform wuzu
Description: These seats allow Muslims to wash their face, head, ears, mouth, nostrils, hands, arms, feet, and ankles in the manner prescribed as wuzu (Arabic: wudu) before doing the formal, ritual prayer of namaz (Arabic: salat). These ablutions ensure a properly purified condition before undertaking prayers to Allah.

Label: See a namaz position
Description: One of the many prayer positions in namaz is prostration, an act of ultimate submission to Allah.  Only men pray at the mosques in Chainpur.  Women do their prayers at home, as do many men unless it is the Friday noon prayer.

Label: After Id prayers (which occur twice a year), a special imam (prayer leader) gives a khutbah (sermon).  The imam might be specially recruited, even from another state.
Visit the Sufi tomb of Mubarak Shah
Description: Certainly, one of the most important religious sites in Chainpur has been the tomb of Mubarak Shah.  Tended by the descendants of this ascetic Muslim intellectual, the onion-domed tomb has stood at the corner of the village's large Jama Masjid (congregational mosque).  Devotees, Hindu and Muslim, frequent this site throughout the year, offering prayers and making requests.

Label: See the performance of dua
Description: While Muslims perform namaz (salat) at specified times of the day such as before dawn, noon, and at sunset, they perform the prayer form of dua at any time they consider it appropriate to supplicate God, cupping their hands together and addressing Allah.

Label: See inside the Sufi’s tomb
Description: With a gravestone at its head and a money box for donations at its foot, the tomb of the Sufi was covered in chadars (cloth sheets) and strings of flowers left by devotees. These devotees celebrated Mubarak Shah's urs (death day celebrations) on the 13th of Jumadas-sani in the Islamic calendar, coming even from neighboring states.  On another night, a pair of dueling qawwali musical troupes would match wits until near dawn in a field behind the fort with an audience of hundreds of nexus dwellers.

Label: Visit the Elephant Well (or is it the Hand Well?)
Description: Between the Jama Masjid and the road, this stepwell has existed for centuries.  Some residents call it “Hath Kua” and claim it is a “hand well” for Muslims to do wuzu (ceremonial cleansing) before namaz (regular prayers) at the neighboring Jama Masjid.  Others say that because the local raja built this to wash his elephant, its name is “Hathi Kua.”  The Hindi and Urdu word Hathi derives from hath since elephants can use the end of their trunks like a hand.

Label: Choose your medicine
Description: Although Prabunath’s family business Sri Mahadev Medical, as written on the rooftop sign has focused on homeopathic medicine, he also has sold allopathic and ayurvedic medicines.  Three generations of his family have run this shop.

Label: Enter the store
Description: Prabunath and his brother staff the counter, sometimes recommending treatments as well as selling medicines prescribed by doctors.  The store’s success had been enough for Prabunath to quit his teaching job and open a new shop in Chainpur’s bazaar.

Label: See Prabunath get interviewed
Description: An American ethnographer interviewed Prabunath about his life and business in Chainpur.

Label: Read the store’s sign
Description: The store’s sign was sponsored by “Him Jewels” which, according to the text at top, was “Made from Himalayan herbs” and an “Ayurvedic soft oil.”  As to the store, the sign declared at right that “Here is the sole seller of English [i.e., Western or allopathic], Yunani, Ayurvedic, and herbal medicine.” “English” referenced Western or allopathic medicine; “Yunani” referenced “Greek” medicine that medieval Arab physicians developed as a system; and “Ayurvedic” medicine originated in ancient South Asia.

Description: The poster of the deities of Lakshmi and Ganesh commonly depicted together and venerated by Hindu businesspeople reflected Pappu and Dhamendra’s devotion.

Label: See Chainpur’s congregational mosque
Description: Although a Sunni Muslim community may use many mosques in its vicinity, most male members would gather for the special Friday noon prayer at the Jama Masjid (congregational mosque).

Label: See Muslims perform wuzu
Description: These seats allow Muslims to wash their face, head, ears, mouth, nostrils, hands, arms, feet, and ankles in the manner prescribed as wuzu (Arabic: wudu) before doing the formal, ritual prayer of namaz (Arabic: salat). These ablutions ensure a properly purified condition before undertaking prayers to Allah.

Label: See a namaz position
Description: One of the many prayer positions in namaz is prostration, an act of ultimate submission to Allah.  Only men pray at the mosques in Chainpur.  Women do their prayers at home, as do many men unless it is the Friday noon prayer.

Visit the Sufi tomb of Mubarak Shah
Description: Certainly, one of the most important religious sites in Chainpur has been the tomb of Mubarak Shah.  Tended by the descendants of this ascetic Muslim intellectual, the onion-domed tomb has stood at the corner of the village's large Jama Masjid (congregational mosque).  Devotees, Hindu and Muslim, frequent this site throughout the year, offering prayers and making requests.

Label: See the performance of dua
Description: While Muslims perform namaz (salat) at specified times of the day such as before dawn, noon, and at sunset, they perform the prayer form of dua at any time they consider it appropriate to supplicate God, cupping their hands together and addressing Allah.

Label: See inside the Sufi’s tomb
Description: With a gravestone at its head and a money box for donations at its foot, the tomb of the Sufi was covered in chadars (cloth sheets) and strings of flowers left by devotees. These devotees celebrated Mubarak Shah's urs (death day celebrations) on the 13th of Jumadas-sani in the Islamic calendar, coming even from neighboring states.  On another night, a pair of dueling qawwali musical troupes would match wits until near dawn in a field behind the fort with an audience of hundreds of nexus dwellers.

Label: Visit the Elephant Well (or is it the Hand Well?)
Description: Between the Jama Masjid and the road, this stepwell has existed for centuries.  Some residents call it “Hath Kua” and claim it is a “hand well” for Muslims to do wuzu (ceremonial cleansing) before namaz (regular prayers) at the neighboring Jama Masjid.  Others say that because the local raja built this to wash his elephant, its name is “Hathi Kua.”  The Hindi and Urdu word Hathi derives from hath since elephants can use the end of their trunks like a hand.

Label: Choose your medicine
Description: Although Prabunath’s family business Sri Mahadev Medical, as written on the rooftop sign has focused on homeopathic medicine, he also has sold allopathic and ayurvedic medicines.  Three generations of his family have run this shop.

Label: Enter the store
Description: Prabunath and his brother staff the counter, sometimes recommending treatments as well as selling medicines prescribed by doctors.  The store’s success had been enough for Prabunath to quit his teaching job and open a new shop in Chainpur’s bazaar.

Label: M to N
Description: This gali (“alley”) leads to a neighborhood with three homes once owned by three brothers.

Label: Visit the family masjid
Description: For untold generations, the family inhabiting this muhalla (neighborhood) has used this small masjid (mosque).  The thin bricks suggest it may have been created during the era of Mughal rule.

Label: Enter the family masjid
Description: Sayyid Azad and Sayyid Karim entered the masjid’s courtyard through this gate.  In the past decade, their family had the mosque newly surfaced and whitewashed.

Label: M to L DETAIL
Description: This street leaves Jama Masjid and heads to Marai.  Households that could afford to do so had water pumped into large plastic water tanks on their roofs to ensure access to water in case of electrical outage, which might happen for many hours a day, or even for the full day.

Label: Visit a masjid
Description: Following the street westward from Jama Masjid, one would come across the Marai muhalla (neighborhood) that included this masjid (mosque).  As was common throughout much of South Asia, this masjid’s aesthetic attraction rests on it various architectural members (such as the notional minars (towers for calling to prayer)), floral patterns, geometric design, and calligraphy.

Label: See calligraphy applied
Description: This painter works to complete the calligraphy above the entrance gate to the newly repainted masjid.  He carefully drew temporary horizontal lines to ensure that he properly renders each Arabic letter as conjoined with others to form the flowing beauty of every word.

Label: AA to BB
Description: A few businesses, like the tailor at left, have positioned themselves along the first few meters of this street leading from Chowk Bazaar before it gave way to residences.  The herringbone-patterned brick paving ensured that the street remained passable even during torrential monsoon rains.

Label: Visit a butcher’s shop (note: graphic image)
Description: M. Bahadur Khan offered a butchered goat to customers while the neighboring shop sold eggs.  Chainpur consumers of meat often see their meals at every stage of preparation, from slaughter onward.  Meanwhile, the small kiosk perched on legs of bricks represented a common type of shop for those without a building.
Notes: photo matched approximately: AA to BB butchers 2000s

Label: Buy fish
Description: Surendra Ram offered fish in this impromptu spot after helping to bring in the catch from one of the several large water reservoirs found around the Chainpur nexus that serve as fish hatcheries.
